transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic? What's been concerning you?

Hi, yeah, thanks. Um, so I'm here because my supervisor basically told me I had to get this checked out or I'm in really big trouble at work. I work at a production plant, right on the line, and you're supposed to stay at your station—like, it's a really strict rule because of all the heavy machinery and forklifts and stuff moving around all the time. 

But I just... I keep leaving my station. I'll just wander off. And it happens during our shift meetings, too. We have these morning meetings in the breakroom before we clock in where everyone sits around the tables, and I'm supposed to just stay put, but I just keep popping up out of my chair. I honestly can't help it. I'll just stand up, or walk to the back of the room, or start pacing, and my supervisor, Gary, he pulled me into the office the other day and said it's becoming a serious safety problem. 

He says I'm a liability because I just take off before I even think about it. And he's right, honestly, I don't even realize I'm doing it until I'm already up and moving. It's like my legs just decide to go before my brain even registers it. So, yeah, if I don't fix this I'm gonna get fired, and I really need this job since I didn't finish high school and it actually pays pretty okay, so... that's what brought me in. I just can't seem to stay in one spot when I'm supposed to.

When you get up and leave your station or start pacing, do you feel like there's an urge or pressure building up inside you that makes you need to move—like you have to get up—or does it just happen automatically without you really feeling any urge beforehand?

Oh, it's definitely... yeah, it's like this crazy pressure. Like, when I try to just stand still by my machine—I run the packaging sealer, which is basically just this long conveyor belt where you literally have to stand in this one little taped-off yellow square on the concrete floor—and if I just stand there, or, oh my gosh, like when we have to sit through those quarterly safety training videos in the breakroom, it literally feels like there is this huge physical pressure just building and building up inside my body. 

It's like... I don't know, it starts in my legs, usually, and then it just creeps up until my whole body is almost humming or buzzing, and I just absolutely have to move. I have to pace, or stretch, or just go do something right then and there. If I don't, I feel like I'm literally going to jump out of my skin. 

It's kind of like holding your breath, you know? Like, you can only hold it for so long before your body just completely takes over and forces you to gasp for air because you just can't take it anymore. That's exactly what it feels like, but with moving. I'll be standing in my square, telling myself, 'Don't move, don't move, Gary is right there,' and the pressure just gets so intense and so uncomfortable that I have to stretch my legs or I'll just start pacing down the line anyway. I just can't keep it pushed down, no matter how hard I try to just stand normal like everyone else.

When you get that pressure and start moving around—like when you pace or stretch—does the uncomfortable feeling go away pretty quickly once you're moving, or does it stay about the same even after you've been up and walking around?

Um, well, it's... I don't really know how to explain it. Like, does it go away quickly? I guess I haven't really timed it or anything. I mean, when I finally start moving, it does feel better, like, instantly better in a way, because I'm finally letting that pressure out. But then, as soon as I stop, it's like it just starts building up all over again. 

So, I don't really know if it goes away completely, or if I just distract myself by walking, you know? Like yesterday, I was walking down to the far end of the plant, near the loading docks—which I wasn't supposed to do, obviously, but I just had to get out of my square—and while I was walking, I felt okay. But the second I stopped to look at one of the pallets, that buzzing feeling in my legs was right back. So I honestly couldn't tell you if the uncomfortable feeling goes away and stays away, or if it just kind of... hides while I'm moving. It's just always there, waiting for me to stand still again. I really haven't paid attention to whether it fully disappears, I just know I feel like I'm going crazy if I don't move.

Going back to when you were a kid—say, in elementary school or middle school—did you have this same problem with not being able to stay still, or is this something that's pretty new for you, like just in the last few years?

Oh, gosh, no, it's definitely not new. Not at all. It’s actually been like this my whole entire life, honestly. Like, if you go all the way back to, gosh, even in elementary school, I was always, always the kid who just could not stay in my seat. 

I remember my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable—she had these little desk clusters, you know, where four desks were pushed together so everyone was facing each other? Well, she eventually had to move my desk completely away from everyone else, like right up next to her big desk, because I just would not sit down. I was always popping up to sharpen my pencil, or look out the window, or just wandering around the room to look at the class pet, which was this little hamster. 

And it wasn't just the moving around, either. I was constantly talking over the teacher, too. Like, she’d be in the middle of a math lesson on the chalkboard and a thought would pop into my head and I’d just say it out loud without even raising my hand or thinking about it. I got so many notes sent home to my mom for blurting things out or for just getting up and wandering around the room during quiet reading time. 

My mom used to get so frustrated with me because it felt like every single week there was a new note or a phone call from the school, and she'd sit me down at the kitchen table and I’d always promise her I’d try harder to just sit still and be quiet. But... I don't know, it was like the exact same pressure I have now at the plant. My legs just wanted to go, and my mouth just wanted to talk, and I couldn't stop it no matter how hard I tried to be good. So yeah, it’s definitely not a new thing at all, it’s just that back then I’d get a yellow slip sent home in my folder, and now I’m about to lose my actual livelihood over it, which is way worse, obviously. But yeah, it's been happening since I was a little kid.

When you were in school, aside from the moving around and blurting things out, did you also have trouble paying attention in class or finishing your schoolwork? Like, would you start an assignment and then get distracted, or have a hard time focusing on what the teacher was saying?

Oh, absolutely. I mean, honestly, that's a huge part of why I didn't even finish high school, to be completely real with you. I just could not focus on anything they were saying or any of the assignments. A teacher would start talking and my brain would just instantly be... somewhere else entirely, thinking about what I was going to do later or just staring at the wall. 

And it’s not just a school thing, either, because it still happens to me all the time right now at the plant, which is so frustrating. Like, they have me doing these inventory logs sometimes, or they want me reading through the new CNC training pages—which is this massive, heavy binder they just drop on your station and expect you to read and actually absorb. And I really, really try. I tell myself, 'Okay, focus, you need to learn this so you don't mess up the machine.' 

So I start out really trying, you know? I'll read the first sentence and I'm locked in. But then, literally after just a few minutes, it's like my brain just completely unplugs itself. The numbers on the inventory sheets or the words in the training manual just completely blur together. I'll be staring right at the page, and my eyes are moving across the lines like I'm reading, but my brain is just gone. And then I get to the bottom of the page and I realize I have absolutely no idea what I just looked at. So I have to keep going back to the top and starting over, over and over again, because I didn't take any of it in. 

It's so embarrassing because people probably think I'm just slow or something, but I'm not! It's just that trying to keep my attention on one piece of paper for more than two minutes is like trying to hold water in my hands. It just slips right through. And it was the exact same way with worksheets and reading assignments back in middle school and high school. I'd just sit there staring at the history book or whatever until the bell rang because I just couldn't keep my mind on it long enough to finish a single paragraph.

Besides the moving around and trouble focusing, do you find yourself doing things without thinking first—like saying things you regret, making quick decisions you later wish you hadn't made, or acting on impulses before you stop to think about the consequences?

Oh my gosh, yes. Yes, all the time. It's actually a huge problem for me right now at the plant, especially with talking. Like, I don't even mean to do it, I swear I don't, but I just... I just cut in on people. Constantly. It's like my mouth just moves on its own before my brain even has a chance to say, 'Hey, wait a second, someone else is talking.' 

Like, just last week—no, wait, it was Tuesday—I was walking past the break area and these two girls from the packaging line were standing there talking about the new PTO policy. And I wasn't even part of the conversation, I was just walking by to get back to my station, but I heard them and I just jumped right in. I literally just inserted myself and started talking over them about how the HR lady explained it wrong. And they just stopped and stared at me, and I could tell they were so annoyed. 

And it happens with my lead all the time, too, which is probably going to get me in serious trouble. We have these morning huddle meetings, right? Where we stand around the big whiteboard before the shift starts. And he'll be in the middle of asking a question to the group, or explaining what the quota is for the day, and before he's even done talking—like, before he's even finished his sentence—I'm already answering him. The words just fall out of my mouth. I just blurt it out. And then he gets this super irritated look on his face, and he'll pause and be like, 'Can I finish, please?' 

And then I feel so stupid and embarrassed, because everybody is looking at me and they're all irritated with me, too. I can hear people sighing or I see them roll their eyes. They probably think I'm just incredibly rude and self-centered, but I'm really not trying to be! It's just that the thought pops into my head and if I don't say it right that exact second, it feels like I'm going to explode. So I just cut people off without meaning to, and then everyone gets mad at me for it. I've tried biting my tongue, literally biting the inside of my cheek, but it just happens so fast I don't even realize I've made a decision to speak until I've already interrupted the whole room.

When you think back to your earliest memories of having this trouble with sitting still and focusing—do you remember how old you were? Was it definitely before you started elementary school, or did it start around first or second grade?

Gosh, exactly how old... um... well, it's hard to remember much before I actually started regular school, like preschool age or whatever, because I was just a little kid running around at home and nobody really expects you to sit at a desk then, you know? But definitely, definitely by the time I was in elementary school. 

Like I was telling you just a few minutes ago, it was already a huge problem then. I was 100% that kid who just could not stay in my seat, from the very beginning. First grade, second grade, all of it. I mean, it wasn't just that one teacher I mentioned, it was pretty much every single year. I'd just be up and wandering around the room, looking at whatever caught my eye, completely ignoring that we were supposed to be in our chairs doing quiet time or whatever. 

And the talking over the teacher—that was just a constant, everyday thing. I just couldn't hold it in. If a thought was in my head, it was coming out of my mouth, even if the teacher was right in the middle of a sentence. So yeah, I'd get those notes sent home constantly for blurting things out and just wandering around the classroom. My mom had this whole stack of them, I swear. It felt like every other day she was pulling another folded-up piece of paper out of my backpack saying I disrupted class again or wouldn't stay seated. So, yeah, definitely early elementary school is when it was already super obvious, because that's when they actually expect you to start sitting still all day, and I just... I just couldn't do it.

When you think about first or second grade—so around age 6 or 7—were you already having these problems with not being able to sit still and blurting things out, or did those problems start a bit later, like in third or fourth grade?

Yeah, exactly, like I was just saying a second ago, it was absolutely right at the beginning. First and second grade, age six or seven, for sure. I know I just mentioned the notes my mom got, but it really did start *that* early. 

My mom actually kept this one specific note from my first-grade teacher—Mrs. Gable, I think her name was? Or maybe Gibson, I can't remember, she had this really big curly hair—but anyway, I was probably six, and the note literally said I was a 'constant disruption' because I just would not stay in my assigned seat. They had those little blue plastic chairs with the metal legs that squeaked super loud on the linoleum, and I was constantly pushing mine back, getting up, walking over to the reading corner, or going to look at the class pet, which was just this boring hamster that slept all day anyway. 

But yeah, even at age six, I was already that kid. I was the one talking over the teacher constantly. Like, Mrs. Gable would be reading a picture book to us on the carpet, and if I knew what was going to happen, I'd just shout it out. I ruined the ending of so many books for the other kids because I couldn't hold it in. So, no, it definitely didn't wait until third or fourth grade to start. It was right there from day one of real school, wandering around the room and blurting things out way before I even knew how to read properly.

Just to make sure I have the timeline right—when you were in first grade, around age 6 or 7, were you already having all of these problems—the not staying in your seat, the blurting things out, and the trouble focusing—or did some of those things start even earlier, like when you were in kindergarten or preschool?

Yeah, I mean, like I've kind of been saying, it's a little tricky to say for sure about preschool or kindergarten. Because, you know, when you're in kindergarten, nobody is really making you sit at a desk all day anyway. You're playing with blocks, you're finger painting, you have recess, you're sitting on the floor. So if I was running around a lot back then, I don't think the teachers really cared as much, or maybe they just thought it was normal little kid stuff. 

But like I told you, once I hit actual elementary school—like first grade, when they suddenly expect you to sit at a desk and actually be quiet—that is exactly when it all became a massive problem. I was absolutely that kid. The one who just could not stay in her seat to save her life. I already mentioned how I was constantly talking over the teacher and getting in trouble for it, but it really was all of those things happening right at the exact same time. 

I'd just be up and wandering around the room, looking at the posters on the wall or seeing what the kid three desks over was doing, and then the teacher would get mad, and then I'd get another one of those notes sent home. God, I hated those notes. I used to try to hide them in the very bottom of my backpack, you know, shoved way down under my crushed-up folders and old lunch bags so my mom wouldn't find them, but she always did. And they always said the exact same thing: she won't stay seated, she's wandering around, she's blurting things out. So, yeah, to answer your question, it was definitely all of those things right there in early elementary school, age six or seven, because that's when the rules changed and I just... I just completely failed at following them.

Oh my gosh, yes. Yes, all the time. It's actually a huge problem for me right now at the plant, especially with talking. Like, I don't even mean to do it, I swear I don't, but I just... I just cut in on people. Constantly. It's like my mouth just moves on its own before my brain even has a chance to say, 'Hey, wait a second, someone else is talking.' 

Like, just last week—no, wait, it was Tuesday—I was walking past the break area and these two girls from the packaging line were standing there talking about the new PTO policy. And I wasn't even part of the conversation, I was just walking by to get back to my station, but I heard them and I just jumped right in. I literally just inserted myself and started talking over them about how the HR lady explained it wrong. And they just stopped and stared at me, and I could tell they were so annoyed. 

And it happens with my lead all the time, too, which is probably going to get me in serious trouble. We have these morning huddle meetings, right? Where we stand around the big whiteboard before the shift starts. And he'll be in the middle of asking a question to the group, or explaining what the quota is for the day, and before he's even done talking—like, before he's even finished his sentence—I'm already answering him. The words just fall out of my mouth. I just blurt it out. And then he gets this super irritated look on his face, and he'll pause and be like, 'Can I finish, please?' 

And then I feel so stupid and embarrassed, because everybody is looking at me and they're all irritated with me, too. I can hear people sighing or I see them roll their eyes. They probably think I'm just incredibly rude and self-centered, but I'm really not trying to be! It's just that the thought pops into my head and if I don't say it right that exact second, it feels like I'm going to explode. So I just cut people off without meaning to, and then everyone gets mad at me for it. I've tried biting my tongue, literally biting the inside of my cheek, but it just happens so fast I don't even realize I've made a decision to speak until I've already interrupted the whole room.

doctor.intent: Determine whether symptoms began in childhood (before age 12) to confirm early-onset ADHD, as the patient has described lifelong symptoms but I need to establish the specific age of onset.
doctor.question: When you think back to your earliest memories of having this trouble with sitting still and focusing—do you remember how old you were? Was it definitely before you started elementary school, or did it start around first or second grade?

patient.answer:
Gosh, exactly how old... um... well, it's hard to remember much before I actually started regular school, like preschool age or whatever, because I was just a little kid running around at home and nobody really expects you to sit at a desk then, you know? But definitely, definitely by the time I was in elementary school. 

Like I was telling you just a few minutes ago, it was already a huge problem then. I was 100% that kid who just could not stay in my seat, from the very beginning. First grade, second grade, all of it. I mean, it wasn't just that one teacher I mentioned, it was pretty much every single year. I'd just be up and wandering around the room, looking at whatever caught my eye, completely ignoring that we were supposed to be in our chairs doing quiet time or whatever. 

And the talking over the teacher—that was just a constant, everyday thing. I just couldn't hold it in. If a thought was in my head, it was coming out of my mouth, even if the teacher was right in the middle of a sentence. So yeah, I'd get those notes sent home constantly for blurting things out and just wandering around the classroom. My mom had this whole stack of them, I swear. It felt like every other day she was pulling another folded-up piece of paper out of my backpack saying I disrupted class again or wouldn't stay seated. So, yeah, definitely early elementary school is when it was already super obvious, because that's when they actually expect you to start sitting still all day, and I just... I just couldn't do it.

doctor.intent: Determine whether symptoms were present before age 12, which is a diagnostic requirement for ADHD (F90.1). The patient has described early elementary school onset, but I need to confirm the symptom onset was clearly before age 12 to meet DSM-5 criteria.
doctor.question: When you think about first or second grade—so around age 6 or 7—were you already having these problems with not being able to sit still and blurting things out, or did those problems start a bit later, like in third or fourth grade?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Even in elementary school, I was the kid who couldn't stay in my seat, talked over the teacher, and got notes sent home for blurting things out or wandering around the room.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking to clarify the exact age when the symptoms started (first/second grade vs third/fourth grade), which directly pertains to whether the onset was prior to age 12.

patient.answer:
Yeah, exactly, like I was just saying a second ago, it was absolutely right at the beginning. First and second grade, age six or seven, for sure. I know I just mentioned the notes my mom got, but it really did start *that* early. 

My mom actually kept this one specific note from my first-grade teacher—Mrs. Gable, I think her name was? Or maybe Gibson, I can't remember, she had this really big curly hair—but anyway, I was probably six, and the note literally said I was a 'constant disruption' because I just would not stay in my assigned seat. They had those little blue plastic chairs with the metal legs that squeaked super loud on the linoleum, and I was constantly pushing mine back, getting up, walking over to the reading corner, or going to look at the class pet, which was just this boring hamster that slept all day anyway. 

But yeah, even at age six, I was already that kid. I was the one talking over the teacher constantly. Like, Mrs. Gable would be reading a picture book to us on the carpet, and if I knew what was going to happen, I'd just shout it out. I ruined the ending of so many books for the other kids because I couldn't hold it in. So, no, it definitely didn't wait until third or fourth grade to start. It was right there from day one of real school, wandering around the room and blurting things out way before I even knew how to read properly.

doctor.question: Just to make sure I have the timeline right—when you were in first grade, around age 6 or 7, were you already having all of these problems—the not staying in your seat, the blurting things out, and the trouble focusing—or did some of those things start even earlier, like when you were in kindergarten or preschool?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Even in elementary school, I was the kid who couldn't stay in my seat, talked over the teacher, and got notes sent home for blurting things out or wandering around the room.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the specific age when my symptoms started, specifically whether they began in first grade (age 6 or 7) or even earlier, which addresses the criterion of symptoms being present prior to age 12.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I mean, like I've kind of been saying, it's a little tricky to say for sure about preschool or kindergarten. Because, you know, when you're in kindergarten, nobody is really making you sit at a desk all day anyway. You're playing with blocks, you're finger painting, you have recess, you're sitting on the floor. So if I was running around a lot back then, I don't think the teachers really cared as much, or maybe they just thought it was normal little kid stuff. 

But like I told you, once I hit actual elementary school—like first grade, when they suddenly expect you to sit at a desk and actually be quiet—that is exactly when it all became a massive problem. I was absolutely that kid. The one who just could not stay in her seat to save her life. I already mentioned how I was constantly talking over the teacher and getting in trouble for it, but it really was all of those things happening right at the exact same time. 

I'd just be up and wandering around the room, looking at the posters on the wall or seeing what the kid three desks over was doing, and then the teacher would get mad, and then I'd get another one of those notes sent home. God, I hated those notes. I used to try to hide them in the very bottom of my backpack, you know, shoved way down under my crushed-up folders and old lunch bags so my mom wouldn't find them, but she always did. And they always said the exact same thing: she won't stay seated, she's wandering around, she's blurting things out. So, yeah, to answer your question, it was definitely all of those things right there in early elementary school, age six or seven, because that's when the rules changed and I just... I just completely failed at following them.
